title: The Region of Convergence
intro: A formula X(s) is only half of a Laplace transform. The other half is the region of the plane where the integral converges, a vertical strip, and two different signals can share one formula and differ only there.

blocks.text: What the ROC is

The region of convergence (ROC) is the set of $s$ for which $\int |x(t)|\,e^{-\sigma t}\,dt$ is finite. As Points of the s-Plane (#/math/laplace-transform/s-plane) showed, that depends only on $\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s$, so the ROC is a vertical strip $\alpha < \operatorname{Re} s < \beta$, where $\alpha$ may be $-\infty$ and $\beta$ may be $+\infty$. For a rational transform, four rules fix it:

items: The ROC contains no poles: at a pole $X(s)$ is infinite, so the integral cannot converge there.
It is bounded by poles, or runs out to infinity: each vertical edge of the strip passes through a pole.
A right-sided signal (zero before some time) has an ROC to the right of its rightmost pole: $\operatorname{Re} s > \max_k \operatorname{Re} p_k$.
A left-sided signal (zero after some time) has an ROC to the left of its leftmost pole. A two-sided signal has a strip between two poles, or no ROC at all.

blocks.text: A signal that is nonzero only for a finite stretch of time is a special case that has the best of everything: it has a finite integral at every $s$, so its ROC is the whole plane.
One formula, two signals

The right-sided exponential $e^{-0.5t}u(t)$ has $X(s) = 1/(s + 0.5)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > -0.5$. The left-sided signal $-e^{-0.5t}u(-t)$ is $-e^{-0.5t}$ for $t < 0$ and $0$ for $t \ge 0$. With $a = 0.5$, its transform is

The upper limit at $t = 0$ gives $-1/(s+a)$ inside the bracket; the lower limit at $t = -\infty$ vanishes only if $e^{-(s+a)t} \to 0$ as $t \to -\infty$, which needs $\operatorname{Re}(s + a) < 0$. The minus sign in front of the integral flips the result to $+1/(s+a)$. As a check, take $s = -1.5 + j$ and integrate numerically: the integral comes to $-0.5 - 0.5j$, and $1/(s + 0.5) = 1/(-1 + j) = -0.5 - 0.5j$.

The same formula, with the opposite region. The surface drawn by the formula is identical in both cases; what changes is which part of it is real. In the viewer below the left-sided signal is solid to the left of the pole at $\sigma = -0.5$ and faded to its right. Change Input signal to decaying exponential and the shading flips: the same landscape with the other half solid.

The shaded strip in the s-plane panel is on the left of the pole. Drag Decay rate a from 0.5 to 1.5: the pole moves to $-1.5$ and the shaded region follows it, while the left-hand part of the surface stays solid. Now watch the imaginary axis: for $a = 0.5$ the axis (the line $\sigma = 0$) lies in the faded part, and the viewer's step The jω axis says the Fourier transform does not exist. Make $a$ negative, $-0.5$ say: the pole is now at $+0.5$, the ROC is $\operatorname{Re} s < 0.5$, and the axis is inside it.

This is why an inverse transform needs the ROC as well as the formula. Without it, $1/(s+0.5)$ could be a signal that decays toward $t = +\infty$ or one that blows up toward $t = -\infty$. The page Inverting the Transform (#/math/laplace-transform/inverse) makes this a working tool.
A strip: the two-sided exponential

The signal $e^{-a|t|}$ with $a > 0$ decays in both directions. Its right half, $e^{-at}u(t)$, needs $\operatorname{Re} s > -a$. Its left half, $e^{at}$ for $t < 0$, transforms to $\int_{-\infty}^{0} e^{(a-s)t}dt = 1/(a - s)$, and needs $\operatorname{Re} s < a$. Both hold on the strip, and there

With $a = 0.5$ the transform is $1/(0.25 - s^2)$, with poles at $\pm 0.5$, mirror images through the imaginary axis, and the ROC is the strip between them, $-0.5 < \sigma < 0.5$. The height at the centre, $s = 0$, is $1/0.25 = 4$. Halfway to the right pole, at $s = 0.25$, it is $1/(0.25 - 0.0625) = 5.33$, rising towards the pole. Make $a$ zero or negative and the strip closes: the viewer then says there is no region of convergence at all and fades the whole surface, because $e^{-a|t|}$ no longer decays in both directions.

In magnitude mode the strip stands out as the solid part between the two poles, which rise as plateaus clipped at height 5, one on each side of the imaginary axis. Probe frequency ω is at 0, so the probe sits at $s = 0$, and its height should read $4$. Drag Decay rate a down toward 0: the strip narrows and the two poles close in on the axis; at $a = 0.1$ the strip is only $0.2$ wide. At $a = 0$ the strip is gone.
A finite signal: the whole plane
The pulse $u(t) - u(t-3)$, which is 1 for 3 seconds, has

An integral over a finite interval is always a finite number, so the ROC is every $s$. The apparent pole at $s = 0$ is not one: there the numerator is also zero, and the value is the area of the pulse, $X(0) = 3$. On the right of the plane the pulse is small: $X(1) = (1 - e^{-3})/1 = 0.950$. On the left it grows, because $e^{-3s}$ blows up: $|X(-1)| = (e^{3} - 1)/1 = 19.1$ and $|X(-3)| = (e^{9} - 1)/3 = 2700$. The signal is short, so it is finite everywhere, but not equally big everywhere.

The whole surface is solid: there is no faded region. The left side climbs to the $+30$ dB ceiling (at $s = -1$ the height is already $25.6$ dB), and the right side is lower. Sweep Probe frequency ω from 0 to 3 and watch the response panel dip to the floor at $\omega = 2.09$ rad/s, where $2\pi/3$ gives the first zero, and again near $4.19$, which is off the probe's range.
Why it matters: stability and causality
When $x(t)$ is the impulse response $h(t)$ of a system, the ROC answers two questions at a glance:

items: Causal (the output never depends on future input): $h(t) = 0$ for $t < 0$, so the ROC is a right half-plane.
Stable in the bounded-input, bounded-output (BIBO) sense: $\int |h(t)|\,dt < \infty$, which is the same as saying the imaginary axis lies in the ROC.
Both at once: the ROC is a right half-plane that contains the imaginary axis, so every pole is in the left half of the plane.

blocks.text: The page Pole Positions and the Time Signal (#/math/laplace-transform/poles-and-time) works through what the poles do to the signal itself.
Problems

blocks.title: Three ROCs
blocks.text: $X(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)(s+3)}$. List every possible ROC. Which gives a stable signal, and which a causal one?
solution: The poles are at $-1$ and $-3$, so the possible regions are $\operatorname{Re} s > -1$, $-3 < \operatorname{Re} s < -1$ and $\operatorname{Re} s < -3$.
Only the first contains the imaginary axis, so it is the stable one; it is also right-sided, hence causal. The middle strip is two-sided, and neither it nor the left half-plane contains the axis.
blocks.answer: Stable and causal: $\operatorname{Re} s > -1$. The other two are neither.

blocks.title: Add two pieces
blocks.text: Find the transform and ROC of $x(t) = e^{-2t}u(t) + e^{t}u(-t)$.
solution: The right piece gives $1/(s+2)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > -2$. The left piece is $e^{t}$ for $t < 0$: $\int_{-\infty}^{0} e^{(1-s)t}dt = 1/(1-s)$, needing $\operatorname{Re} s < 1$. Together $X(s) = \dfrac{1}{s+2} + \dfrac{1}{1-s} = \dfrac{3}{(s+2)(1-s)}$ on $-2 < \operatorname{Re} s < 1$, a strip containing the imaginary axis.

blocks.title: A finite signal
blocks.text: What is the ROC of $x(t) = \delta(t+1) + \delta(t-1)$?
solution: $X(s) = e^{s} + e^{-s} = 2\cosh s$. It is finite for every $s$ (no poles), so the ROC is the whole plane.
